2027: BIOCORE presented by Haas Kickoff is Saturday, January 9, 2027. This season’s FIRST CANOPY theme is nature, and the game will dig into what sustains life on Earth. The game reveal streams at 11 a.m. Central on FIRST’s YouTube channel.

Fe Iron Tigers

Frenship Engineering’s FIRST Robotics Competition team from Wolfforth, Texas. We started in 2016 with 16 students, and Frenship Engineering has since set the gold standard for high school engineering in West Texas. Every January we get a brand-new game, and a few weeks later we’re competing with a robot we designed, built, wired, and programmed ourselves.

Our mission: STEM at homeWest Texas is farm and ranch country, and students here don’t always have access to the latest technology. That’s why we focus on spreading STEM in our own schools and communities, building opportunities right here at home instead of trying to reach around the globe.

Robots and seasons

Each season’s game is different, so each robot is built from scratch. Here’s what we’ve built and how it went. For match results, rankings, and videos from every event, see our team page on The Blue Alliance.

  1. 2026

    Bruno

    REBUILT

    Built to collect the game’s yellow balls in bulk, with rows of roller wheels feeding a hopper that holds several at once.

    Competed at the FIRST in Texas Waco District Event in March and the Amarillo District Event in April, where the team won the Engineering Inspiration Award for the second year in a row and advanced to the FIRST in Texas District Championship. For the third year in a row, students nominated Coach James Holloway for the Woodie Flowers Finalist Award.

  2. 2025

    Squidward

    REEFSCAPE

    Squidward was built around a tall elevator for the REEFSCAPE season.

    Won the Engineering Inspiration Award at the FIRST in Texas Amarillo District Event, earning an invitation to the FIRST in Texas District Championship to compete for the state Engineering Inspiration Award. Students also nominated Coach James Holloway for the Woodie Flowers Finalist Award.

  3. 2024

    Terry D. Rex

    CRESCENDO

    Terry D. Rex was built with two tall climbing hooks and a belt-driven pivoting arm.

    At the Amarillo District Event, students nominated Coach James Holloway for the Woodie Flowers Finalist Award.

  4. 2023

    Titus

    CHARGED UP

    A swerve-drive robot with an articulated claw on an elbow-and-wrist arm. Built in three weeks and programmed in two, Titus could even push itself back upright after being knocked over.

    Picked by the #4 alliance at both Waco and Amarillo. Finished fourth of 40 teams at Waco, took the #1 alliance to the wire in Amarillo, and missed a state championship invite by just 10 points.

  5. 2021

    Decimator 2.0

    INFINITE RECHARGE

    After a virtual season cost the team many members, the students who stayed rebuilt the program and earned a spot at the Texas State UIL Competition with Decimator 2.0.

    Won the Texas Cup on the winning alliance with alliance captain Team 3310, Black Hawk Robotics, and Team 9889, the Robowranglers’ off-season team associated with Team 148.

  6. 2016

    ROVER

    FIRST STRONGHOLD

    Our first robot, built by the 16 students who founded the team with Coach James Holloway. ROVER used its arm to grab the game’s boulders and carry them across the castle field.

How we’re organized

FRC isn’t just about building a robot. It’s about running a small engineering firm. So instead of a president and vice president, we use an Engineering Matrix Organization, the same structure modern engineering companies use.

Leadership is split into two equal, interdependent groups. Domain Leads mentor their sub-teams and own the technical quality: the how. Project Integrators work across every sub-team to manage schedule, strategy, and communication: the what and the when.

The result is real collaboration. Mechanical can’t build without CAD, and programmers can’t test without both, so the structure keeps everyone talking. Leadership is shared so nobody burns out during build season, and teaching younger members is part of every leader’s job.

Domain Leads

The technical mentors

  • Design & CAD LeadJoey DuffLeads all 3D modeling in Autodesk Fusion 360, trains new members in CAD, manages version control, and makes sure every mechanism is fully modeled before anyone cuts metal.
  • Fabrication & Shop LeadBenjamin TeelOwns the physical build. Trains students on shop tools, enforces safety, and oversees manufacturing the robot from the CAD files.
  • Controls & Software LeadBraxton PottsOwns the robot’s brain and nervous system. Teaches programming, oversees wiring schematics, and tests autonomous routines and driver controls.

Project Integrators

The cross-functional managers

  • Systems IntegratorKwabena Oduro-FirikyiRuns the master build schedule so CAD finishes in time for fabrication, and fabrication leaves room for the electronics.
  • Strategy Analyst & Drive CoachSean BobbOur expert on the game manual. Works with every sub-team to maximize scoring and avoid penalties, then leads the drive team at competitions.
  • Enterprise & Outreach ManagerTeagan MalletteRuns the business side: sponsor updates, community outreach, and our FIRST Impact Award submission.

Outreach and joining

We’re building a K–12 STEM pipeline in West Texas, and we have a no-cuts policy: curiosity is the only requirement to join.

In the community

  • Airbattles drone competitionOur students designed Airbattles to get younger students excited about STEM, and they build and run it every year, with elementary, middle school, and high school divisions. It’s made possible by Texas Tech University’s Whitacre College of Engineering and an endowment from the Evelyn Davies Foundation.
  • FIRST in our feeder schoolsWe founded and mentor FIRST Tech Challenge teams in Frenship’s middle schools, help host LEGO events for elementary students, and built LEGO competition tables for every Frenship elementary school.
  • New teams across the regionWe partnered with and helped establish Panther Pride #11200, the first FRC team we’ve helped launch, and we support other local teams from Monterey High School and Lubbock High School. We’re also working with the Texas Tech Robotics Association to build a practice field for FRC teams in our area.
  • Demos and STEM daysYou’ll find our robot at the Science Spectrum, STEM fairs, and community events.
  • ServiceWe’re running our 2nd annual Stuffed Animal Drive for the UMC surgical unit, where the animals comfort children going into surgery. Last year we collected more than 200, and this year we’ve teamed up with schools and organizations across our community to make it even bigger.

How to join

  1. Come to fall workshops.
    Weekly workshops in the fall teach tools, safety, CAD, coding, and electronics. They’re open to high school and middle school students.
  2. Find your place on the team.
    Join a sub-team in design, fabrication, controls, strategy, or outreach, and grow into a leadership role in our Engineering Matrix Organization.
  3. Build, compete, and travel.
    Kickoff is in January, and competition season takes us to district events across Texas.

There’s a job for everyone:

  • Mechanical build
  • Programming
  • CAD and design
  • Electrical
  • Drive team
  • Scouting and strategy
  • Business and media
